questions.q: Which HTTP header carries credentials for both Basic Authentication and OAuth 2.0?
options: Content-Type
Accept
Authorization
Cache-Control
questions.explain: Both methods send credentials via the Authorization header.

questions.q: Is base64 encoding the same thing as encryption?
options: Yes, base64 is a strong encryption algorithm
No — base64 is reversible encoding; it provides no protection on its own
Yes, but only for OAuth tokens
Base64 is unrelated to authentication entirely
questions.explain: Base64 is just an encoding scheme, trivially reversible, not encryption.

questions.q: What is a practical advantage of an OAuth 2.0 bearer token over a Basic Auth password?
options: It never needs to be sent at all
It can be revoked independently and naturally expires, without changing the account password
It is always shorter than a password
It works without HTTPS
questions.explain: Tokens can be revoked and expire on their own, unlike a reused password.

questions.q: What constraint makes Basic Authentication unusable for some Oracle Fusion users?
options: Basic Authentication cannot be used with users set up for multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Basic Authentication requires a credit card on file
Basic Authentication only works on weekends
There is no such constraint
questions.explain: Basic Authentication conflicts with MFA-enabled users for Fusion REST calls.

questions.q: What actually protects a Basic Authentication header in transit?
options: The base64 encoding itself
Sending every call over HTTPS
Using a short password
Nothing can protect it
questions.explain: HTTPS, not base64, is what actually protects the credentials in transit.
